questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a country Ive never been to and also go to a good university.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Really great overall. One of the best experiences of my life.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UTokyo sends a lot (maybe even too much) information in advance and everything is organised really well.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had a welcome event and everything related to the university and courses was explained there. We also got divided into smaller groups with UTokyo students (buddies) that were also always there to answer questions. There is also an office for exchange students on both campuses where you can talk to someone in person if there are any questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are two or three different dorms for UTokyo exchange students. The two main ones are Komaba and Mejirodai. The Komaba dorm is on Komaba Campus near Shibuya and Mejirodai is closer to Hongo Campus but not located directly on any of the campuses.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There are shared kitchens in all dorms. Komaba is convenient because it is on Komaba Campus and you can walk to the canteen in 5 mins, which is also open in the evenings. There are no meal plans available.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would very much recommend the Komaba dorm. Facilities are a bit more outdated than in Mejirodai but the location is unbeatable. Its also the more social dorm walking home from Shibuya after going out is a real benefit. Its especially convenient if you take a lot of courses on Komaba campus because you can just walk to class in 5 mins. But even if I had all classes on Hongo campus I would choose Komaba because the location is just perfect. In Komaba Main and Annex you have your own bathroom which is really nice. In Komaba B, C, and D you have to share a bathroom, which I have heard is not that great, but I would have still preferred B, C, and D over living somewhere else. It is really a great place to live and socialise. Living in walking distance to the canteen and many great restaurants is also amazing.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You can look at the course catalogue beforehand but it is only finalised right before classes start. You get a two week trial period to sit in all the courses and then you register by the end of the two weeks. This is also recommended because many classes expect you to be there from the very beginning.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The registration process was explained on orientation day and you could also reach out to your UTokyo buddies or the student office at all times.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all of the classes I wanted and also heard that the spots are overall not that competitive, so you should be able to get the courses you want.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take the time to check out all the classes you are considering. Some are very different from the course description, so its good to get a feel for the course and lecturer before choosing it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level is overall quite low in the courses for exchange students aka the english speaking courses. Japanese students typically take a lot more courses than the exchange students so the individual level of each course is quite low and most of them only consist of a 1.5-2 hour lecture a week. Most classes take attendance, which is a bit annoying, but the requirements to get an A in a course are pretty low and the final exam is often just a short report or project.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Its similar I guess. You have a lecturer that gives a lecture. Perhaps there is a bit more participation expected from the students at UTokyo because some count participation as part of the grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: I took Gender Data Gap, Environmental Economics, Development Economics, Chinese Diplomacy, Japanese Foreign Policy, and Start Up and Venture Capital.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I liked Gender Data Gap, we talked about gender issues in data and it was a very interactive course, but no prior experience with data work was expected. The final grade consisted of a presentation and final report. Environmental and Development were okay, the level was quite low, and you just had to write a final report. Chinese Diplomacy and Japanese Foreign Policy were interesting if you are generally interested in the subjects. In both the final grade consists of the presentation of a paper and a final report. Start Up and Venture Capital was very fun. The lecturer used to be a VC head in Japan and has a lot of practical experience. We had to develop our own start up in groups which was super fun.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing really unexpected. You do have to enrol in Japanese health insurance, even if you are already insured back home, but it is pretty cheap.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: It was pretty much how I expected. I went to eat out every meal (also a lot of Kombini and Canteen), but it is of course a bit more expensive than only cooking at home. Although it does not make that big of a difference in Japan and the food is so great. I also travelled quite a bit around Japan and China, which can get quite expensive as Shinkansen and flights are not that cheap. But if you can its so worth it! Japan is such a beautiful country and travelling around East Asia is also great.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are a lot of activities at UTokyo. They are divided into clubs and circles. Clubs are very competitive and train 4-6 times a week, so I would only join if you are up for this and already an expert at the sport/ activity. Circles are pretty chill and you can join at pretty much any level. I joined the Taekwando circle as a beginner, which was very fun. The only difficulty might be finding a club/ circle that accepts English speaking students, as a lot of them are in Japanese. But you can get a feel for this from the way they are presented on the website. There is also an info event for a lot of English speaking clubs and circles at the beginning of the semester, which I would really recommend going to!

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join any circle you are interested in to learn something new and meet Japanese students!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go around Tokyo and Japan as much as you can there is so, so much to see! I went to Kyoto, Osaka, Nikko, Nagano (Shiga Kogen to ski), Hakone, and Okinawa in Japan. All were really great. I also went to Shanghai and Beijing in China which was also super fun. I would also recommend to stay in Japan a bit longer after the semester ends to travel more. We can live in the dorm until the end of March in the winter semester, which is really convenient.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Everything in Japan is so convenient and easy to understand. Japanese people are very polite and helpful so if you have any questions there is always someone to help.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I became friends with my UTokyo buddies and met other local students through joining circles.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Most Japanese people do not speak English very well. Its not a big problem in daily life but it makes it a bit harder to immerse yourself in Japanese culture, because its harder to fully participate if you dont know the language.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The. food. is. amazing. !!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Go to the canteen a lot (and get a COOP membership early on for cheaper meals). Go around Tokyo and Japan as much as you can. Max out your stay in Japan by staying until the end of the semester (if possible)!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do not expect a crazy academic challenge and go more for the experience and culture! Its such an amazing opportunity we get to have by going on exchange.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting amazing people. There were other exchange students from all over the world and I made really great new friends. Also meeting Japanese people and hearing about their experiences and world views was very interesting.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Leaving and saying goodbye :(

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I would 100% go again (also to UTokyo over other Japanese universities), so I think you will have the best time as well!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
